paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Bucket is the only one in the family with a job, and he is paid very little. The family can buy only bread, potatoes and cabbage.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Bucket was the only one in the family with a job. He worked in a toothpaste factory. He sat all day and screwed the little caps on the tubes of toothpaste. But a man who does this work is never paid much. Mr Bucket worked hard and fast, but he could never make enough money to buy even half of the things his big family needed. There was not even enough money for proper food. They could buy only bread and margarine for breakfast, boiled potatoes and cabbage for lunch, and cabbage soup for supper. Sundays were a little better. They had the same food, but everyone could have a second helping, so they looked forward to Sundays.

paragraphs.context: Only once a year, on his birthday, did Charlie Bucket ever get to taste
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie gets one small chocolate bar each year, on his birthday. He eats it in tiny bites, so that it lasts more than a month.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie got a little chocolate only once a year, on his birthday. The whole family saved up their money for that day, and Charlie was given one small chocolate bar to eat by himself. He kept it in a small wooden box and treasured it as if it were a bar of gold. For the next few days he only looked at it and never touched it. At last, when he could not wait any longer, he pulled back a tiny bit of the paper at one corner, so that a tiny bit of chocolate showed. Then he took a tiny nibble, just enough to let the sweet taste spread slowly over his tongue. The next day he took another tiny nibble, and so on. In this way he made his sixpenny bar of birthday chocolate last more than a month.

paragraphs.context: owned by a man called Mr Willy Wonka, the greatest inventor and maker
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Willy Wonka's factory is the largest and most famous chocolate factory in the world. It is in Charlie's town, and the air near it smells of melting chocolate.
paragraphs.simple: It was not just an ordinary big chocolate factory. It was the largest and most famous in the whole world. It was Wonka's Factory, owned by a man called Mr Willy Wonka, the greatest inventor and maker of chocolates there has ever been. And what a wonderful place it was! It had huge iron gates, and a high wall around it. Smoke came out of its chimneys, and there were strange whizzing sounds from deep inside. Outside the walls, for half a mile in every direction, the air smelled of the heavy rich smell of melting chocolate.

paragraphs.context: They were as shrivelled as prunes, and as bony as skeletons
paragraphs.mainIdea: The four grandparents are very old and spend all day in bed. They are happy only when Charlie visits them in the evening.
paragraphs.simple: All four old people were over ninety. They were dried up like prunes, and as thin as skeletons. All day, until Charlie came, they lay close together in their one bed, two at each end. They wore nightcaps to keep their heads warm, and they slept a little with nothing to do. But when they heard the door open and heard Charlie say good evening, all four sat up, and their old faces lit up with smiles. They loved the little boy. He was the only bright thing in their lives, and they looked forward to his visits all day. His mother and father often came in too and stood by the door to listen to the stories. For about half an hour every night, this room became a happy place, and the family forgot that it was hungry and poor.

paragraphs.simple: Grandpa Joe goes on slowly so that Charlie will not miss a word. Mr Willy Wonka can make marshmallows that taste of violets, and rich caramels that change colour every ten seconds while you suck them. He can make little feathery sweets that melt in your mouth the moment you put them between your lips. He can make chewing-gum that never loses its taste. He can make sugar balloons that you can blow up to a huge size before you pop them with a pin and gobble them up. And by a very secret method, he can make lovely blue birds' eggs with black spots on them. When you put one in your mouth, it slowly gets smaller and smaller, until there is nothing left except a tiny pink sugary baby bird on the tip of your tongue.

paragraphs.context: the whole palace began to melt, and then it sank slowly to the ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: Prince Pondicherry's chocolate palace melts in the hot sun. The prince wakes up in a lake of chocolate.
paragraphs.simple: But Mr Wonka was right. Soon after this, there was a very hot day with a boiling sun. The whole palace began to melt, and then it slowly sank to the ground. The crazy prince had been dozing in the living room. When he woke up, he found himself swimming in a huge brown sticky lake of chocolate.

paragraphs.context: All the other chocolate makers, you see, had begun to grow jealous
paragraphs.mainIdea: Other chocolate makers sent spies into Mr Wonka's factory to steal his secrets.
paragraphs.simple: Grandpa Joe says that all the other chocolate makers had begun to feel jealous of the wonderful sweets that Mr Wonka was making. They began to send spies to steal his secret recipes. The spies took jobs in the Wonka factory and pretended to be ordinary workers. While they were there, each one of them found out exactly how a certain special thing was made.

paragraphs.context: The chimneys stopped smoking, the machines stopped whirring, and from then on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka sends everyone home and closes the factory. After that, nobody sees him.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka told all the workers that he was sorry, but they would have to go home. Then he shut the main gates and fastened them with a chain. Suddenly the giant chocolate factory became silent and empty. The chimneys stopped smoking and the machines stopped. From then on, not a single chocolate or sweet was made. Not a soul went in or out, and even Mr Willy Wonka himself disappeared completely.

paragraphs.context: The picture showed a nine-year-old boy who was so enormously fat he looked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Augustus Gloop, a very fat boy, finds the first Golden Ticket. His town is very excited.
paragraphs.simple: On the very next day, the first Golden Ticket was found by a boy called Augustus Gloop. Mr Bucket's evening newspaper had a large picture of him on the front page. He was a nine-year-old boy and so very fat that he looked as if he had been blown up with a strong pump. Big soft folds of fat stuck out from every part of his body. His face was like a huge ball of dough, with two small greedy eyes like currants. The newspaper said that his town had gone wild with excitement. Flags were flying from all the windows, children had a holiday from school, and there was a parade to honour him.

paragraphs.context: Fully grown women were seen going into sweet shops and buying ten Wonka bars
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everybody in the world rushes to buy Wonka chocolate and find a Golden Ticket. Some people do very silly things.
paragraphs.simple: Now the whole world seemed to go mad buying chocolate, and everybody looked for the last tickets. Grown women went into sweet shops and bought ten Wonka bars at a time. They tore off the wrappers at once and looked eagerly underneath for a glint of gold paper. Children took hammers and smashed their piggy banks and ran to the shops with handfuls of money. In one city, a famous gangster robbed a bank of a thousand pounds and spent all of it on Wonka bars that afternoon. When the police came into his house to arrest him, they found him sitting on the floor with mountains of chocolate around him, ripping off the wrappers with the blade of a long dagger. In Russia, a woman called Charlotte Russe said she had found the second ticket, but it was a clever fake. The famous English scientist, Professor Foulbody, invented a machine that could tell you at once if there was a Golden Ticket under the wrapper of a chocolate bar. The machine had a metal arm that shot out and grabbed anything with gold in it. For a moment it looked like the answer to everything. But while the Professor was showing off the machine at the sweet counter of a big shop, the arm shot out and grabbed the gold filling in the back tooth of a duchess who was standing near. There was an ugly scene, and the crowd smashed the machine.

paragraphs.context: the toothpaste factory, the place where Mr Bucket worked, suddenly went bust
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Bucket's factory closes, and he loses his job. The family now has even less food.
paragraphs.simple: The toothpaste factory where Mr Bucket worked suddenly went bust and had to close. Mr Bucket quickly tried to find another job, but he had no luck. In the end, the only way he could earn a few pennies was by shovelling snow in the streets. But that was not enough to buy even a quarter of the food that seven people needed. Things became very bad. Breakfast was now one slice of bread for each person, and lunch was maybe half a boiled potato.

paragraphs.context: he began to make little changes here and there in some of the things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Because he is so hungry, Charlie does things slowly and carefully to save his strength.
paragraphs.simple: Now Charlie stayed very calm. Small children often seem to have a strange wisdom in hard times, and he began to make small changes in some of the things he did, to save his strength. In the mornings, he left the house ten minutes earlier so that he could walk slowly to school and never have to run. During break, he sat quietly in the classroom and rested while the other children rushed outside and threw snowballs and wrestled in the snow. He did everything slowly and carefully now, so that he would not get too tired.

paragraphs.context: and oh, the joy of being able to cram large pieces of something sweet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie buys a chocolate bar and eats it fast. After so much hunger, he is very happy.
paragraphs.simple: The man behind the counter looked fat and well fed. He had big lips, fat cheeks and a very fat neck. The fat around his neck bulged out over his collar like a rubber ring. He turned and reached behind him for the chocolate bar, then he handed it to Charlie. Charlie grabbed it, quickly tore off the wrapper and took an enormous bite. Then he took another bite, and another. How wonderful it was to push large pieces of something sweet and solid into his mouth! It was pure happiness to fill his mouth with rich solid food.

paragraphs.context: There was a peculiar floating sensation coming over him, as though he were floating
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is so shocked and happy that he feels dizzy and light.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie had not moved. He had not even taken the Golden Ticket off the chocolate. He stood very still and held it tightly with both hands while the crowd pushed and shouted around him. He felt quite dizzy. It was a strange floating feeling, as if he were floating up in the air like a balloon. His feet did not seem to touch the ground at all. He could hear his heart thumping loudly somewhere in his throat.

paragraphs.context: Then the old man took a deep breath, and suddenly, with no warning whatsoever
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandpa Joe is so happy about the Golden Ticket that he jumps out of bed and dances.
paragraphs.simple: Very slowly, a big happy smile spread over Grandpa Joe's face, and he looked straight at Charlie. The colour rushed to his cheeks. His eyes were wide open and shining with joy, and in the middle of each eye, in the black part, a little spark of wild excitement was slowly dancing. Then the old man took a deep breath, and suddenly, with no warning at all, it was like an explosion inside him. He threw up his arms and shouted Yippee. At the same time, his long thin body rose up out of the bed, and his bowl of soup went flying into the face of Grandma Josephine. In one great jump, this old man of ninety-six and a half, who had not been out of bed for the last twenty years, jumped onto the floor and started doing a winner's dance in his pyjamas.

paragraphs.context: I am preparing other surprises that are even more marvellous and more fantastic
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the letter on the Golden Ticket. It tells the winner when to come to the factory and what to bring.
paragraphs.simple: Greetings to you, the lucky finder of this Golden Ticket, from Mr Willy Wonka! I shake you warmly by the hand! Great things are waiting for you. Many wonderful surprises are waiting for you. For now, I invite you to come to my factory and be my guest for one whole day, you and all the others who are lucky enough to find my Golden Tickets. I, Willy Wonka, will show you around the factory myself and show you everything there is to see. Afterwards, when it is time to leave, a line of large trucks will take you home. The trucks will be full of enough good things to eat to last you and your whole household for many years. If you ever run out, you only have to come back to the factory and show this Golden Ticket, and I will be happy to fill your cupboard again with whatever you want. In this way, you will have tasty bits of food for the rest of your life. But this is by no means the most exciting thing that will happen on the day of your visit. I am getting ready other surprises that are even more wonderful and more fantastic for you and for all my Golden Ticket holders. They will delight, interest, surprise and confuse you beyond measure. In your wildest dreams you could not imagine such things. Just wait and see! Now, here are your instructions. The day I have chosen is the first day of February. On this day, and no other, you must come to the factory gates at ten o'clock sharp in the morning. Do not be late! You may bring one or two members of your own family to look after you and to make sure that you do not get into mischief. One more thing: be sure to have this ticket with you, or you will not be let in.

paragraphs.context: He kept making quick jerky little movements with his head, cocking it this way
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka looks very clever and moves quickly, like a squirrel.
paragraphs.simple: And how clever he looked! He was quick and sharp and full of life. He kept making quick little jerky movements with his head, turning it this way and that, and taking in everything with his bright twinkling eyes. He moved as quickly as a squirrel, like a quick clever old squirrel from the park.

paragraphs.context: The children and their parents were too flabbergasted to speak
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children and parents are so surprised by the chocolate river that they cannot speak.
paragraphs.simple: The children and their parents were too surprised to speak. They were very shocked. They did not know what to think. Their eyes were dazzled. The size of it all was too much for them. They just stood and stared.

paragraphs.context: is made of a new kind of soft, minty sugar that I’ve just invented
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka explains how the waterfall mixes the chocolate. He tells them that the trees, the bushes and the grass can all be eaten.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka goes on: the waterfall is most important! It mixes the chocolate. It churns it up, pounds it and beats it, and makes it light and frothy. No other factory in the world mixes its chocolate by waterfall, but it is the only way to do it well. He asks if they like his trees and his lovely bushes, and he says that he hates ugliness. Of course they can all be eaten, and each one is made of something different and delicious. He asks if they like his meadows, his grass and his buttercups. The grass they are standing on is made of a new kind of soft sugar that tastes of mint, which he has just invented. He calls it swudge. He asks them to try a blade of it, and he says it is delicious.

paragraphs.context: I found the little Oompa-Loompas living in tree houses
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka says that in Loompaland the Oompa-Loompas lived in tree houses, ate horrible food, and wanted cacao beans more than anything.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka tells them about Loompaland. He says it is a terrible country, with nothing but thick jungles full of the most dangerous beasts in the world: hornswogglers, snozzwangers and wicked whangdoodles. A whangdoodle would eat ten Oompa-Loompas for breakfast and come back for a second helping. When he went there, the Oompa-Loompas were living in tree houses, to get away from those beasts. They were living on green caterpillars, which tasted horrible. They spent every moment of their days in the treetops, looking for other things to mash up with the caterpillars to make them taste better, such as red beetles, leaves, and the bark of the bong-bong tree. The food they wanted more than any other was the cacao bean, but they could not get it. They were lucky to find three or four cacao beans a year. They dreamed about cacao beans all night and talked about them all day. If you said the word cacao to an Oompa-Loompa, his mouth would start to run with water. The cacao bean grows on the cacao tree, and all chocolate is made from it. Mr Wonka says you cannot make chocolate without the cacao bean.

paragraphs.context: So I shipped them all over here, every man, woman, and child in the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka says how he brought the Oompa-Loompas to his factory. They work hard, love songs, and like jokes.
paragraphs.simple: So Mr Wonka sent all the Oompa-Loompas over to his country, every man, woman and child. He says it was easy. He smuggled them over in large packing cases with holes in them, and they all got there safely. They are wonderful workers. They all speak English now. They love dancing and music, and they are always making up songs. They are rather mischievous and like jokes. They still wear the same kind of clothes that they wore in the jungle, and they insist on that. The men wear only deerskins, the women wear leaves, and the children wear nothing at all. The women use fresh leaves every day.

paragraphs.context: the wretched boy was being sucked closer and closer towards the mouth of one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Augustus Gloop falls in the chocolate river and is pulled into a pipe.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Gloop said he was doing something. He was taking off his jacket and getting ready to jump into the chocolate. But while he was doing this, the poor boy was being pulled closer and closer to the mouth of one of the great pipes that hung down into the river. Then all at once the strong pull took hold of him completely, and he was pulled under the chocolate and into the mouth of the pipe.

paragraphs.context: I tried it on an Oompa-Loompa yesterday in the Testing Room
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka's Hair Toffee is too strong. It made an Oompa-Loompa grow a very long beard.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka tells Veruca that a beard would suit her very well. But the mixture is not quite right yet. He has made it too strong, and it works too well. Yesterday he tried it on an Oompa-Loompa in the Testing Room. At once a huge black beard started shooting out of his chin. It grew so fast that soon it was trailing all over the floor like a thick hairy carpet. It grew faster than they could cut it, and in the end they had to use a lawn mower. But he says he will soon get the mixture right. When he does, no boy or girl will have to go about with a bald head.

paragraphs.context: Her body was swelling up and changing shape at such a rate
paragraphs.mainIdea: Violet Beauregarde turns into a giant blueberry after chewing the gum.
paragraphs.simple: But now nobody could save her. Her body was getting bigger and changing shape so fast that in one minute it became a huge round blue ball. It was a giant blueberry. All that was left of Violet Beauregarde was a tiny pair of legs and a tiny pair of arms sticking out of the great round fruit, and a little head on top.

paragraphs.context: You do a great big long rude burp, and up comes the gas
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka explains how to come down after a Fizzy Lifting Drink. An Oompa-Loompa once went up and was never seen again.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka says you do a burp, a great big long rude burp, and up comes the gas and down comes you. But he says you must not drink it outside, because nobody knows how high you will be carried. Once he gave some to an old Oompa-Loompa in the back yard, and the Oompa-Loompa went up and up and out of sight. It was very sad. He never saw him again.

paragraphs.context: Mrs Salt bent further forward to get a closer look
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs Salt looks down the hole in the Nut Room, and the squirrels push her in.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs Salt bent forward to see better. She was on her knees at the edge of the hole, with her head down and her enormous behind sticking up in the air like a giant mushroom. It was a dangerous way to be. She needed only one tiny push, one gentle nudge in the right place, and that is just what the squirrels gave her. Over she fell, into the hole head first, screaming like a parrot.

paragraphs.context: The lift rushed on at the speed of a rocket
paragraphs.mainIdea: The glass lift goes very fast, up and down, and makes Charlie's tummy feel strange.
paragraphs.simple: The lift went on as fast as a rocket. Now it began to climb. It shot up and up on a steep sloping path, as if it were climbing a very steep hill. Then suddenly, as if it had come to the top of the hill and gone over a cliff, it dropped like a stone. Charlie felt his tummy come right up into his throat.

paragraphs.context: The photographs are then split up into millions of tiny little pieces
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka explains how a television works. He says a picture is broken into tiny pieces and put together again.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka asks if they know how ordinary television works. At one end, where the picture is taken, there is a large camera that photographs something. The photographs are split up into millions of tiny pieces, so small that you cannot see them, and electricity shoots these pieces out into the sky. In the sky they whizz about until they hit the antenna on the roof of somebody's house. Then they flash down the wire into the back of the television set. There they are jiggled and joggled around until every one of the millions of tiny pieces is back in its right place, like a jigsaw puzzle, and the photograph appears on the screen.

paragraphs.context: the lift had shot right up through the roof of the factory
paragraphs.mainIdea: The glass lift breaks through the factory roof and flies into the sky.
paragraphs.simple: Then suddenly there was a crash and a huge noise of breaking wood and broken tiles from above their heads. Grandpa Joe shouted that it was the end and they were done for, but Mr Wonka said no, they were through and out. The lift had shot right up through the roof of the factory, and now it was rising into the sky like a rocket. The sunshine was pouring in through the glass roof. In five seconds they were a thousand feet up in the sky.

paragraphs.context: So I have to have a child. I want a good sensible loving child
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Wonka explains why he wants to give his factory to a child, not to a grown-up.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Wonka says he is an old man, much older than Charlie thinks. He cannot go on for ever. He has no children and no family at all. Someone must run the factory when he is too old, if only for the Oompa-Loompas. Thousands of clever men would give anything for the chance to take over, but he does not want that kind of person. He does not want a grown-up at all. A grown-up will not listen to him or learn, and will try to do things his own way and not his. So he has to have a child. He wants a good, sensible, loving child to whom he can tell all his most precious sweet-making secrets while he is still alive.

sentences.context: There wasn't any question of them being able to buy a better house
sentences.simple: They could not buy a better house, or even one more bed to sleep in.
sentences.grammar: 'There wasn't any question of + -ing' means 'it was not possible to ...'; here, 'to buy a better house'.

sentences.context: he would see other children taking bars of creamy chocolate
sentences.simple: Many times a day he saw other children take bars of chocolate out of their pockets and eat them in a greedy way. Of course, that was very painful for him.
sentences.grammar: 'Would' here is not about the future; it shows something that happened again and again in the past.

sentences.context: when he could stand it no longer, he would peel back a tiny bit
sentences.simple: At last, when he could not wait any longer, he would pull back a little of the paper at one corner so that a little chocolate showed. Then he would take a tiny bite, just enough to let the sweet taste spread slowly over his tongue.
sentences.grammar: 'Could stand it no longer' means 'could not wait any longer', and 'would' shows what he did again and again.

sentences.context: He has some really fantastic inventions up his sleeve
sentences.simple: Mr Willy Wonka has some really wonderful new inventions that nobody knows about yet.
sentences.grammar: 'Up his sleeve' is an idiom for 'kept secret'. The speaker puts 'Mr Willy Wonka has' at the end to make the point stronger.

sentences.context: in some marvellous way to grow quite young again
sentences.simple: In some wonderful way, he seemed to become young again.
sentences.grammar: 'Seemed to + verb' means 'looked as if'; 'grow' here means 'become'.

sentences.context: have workers streaming in and out of the gates in the mornings and evenings
sentences.simple: Every factory has workers coming in and out of the gates in the morning and in the evening, except Wonka's!
sentences.grammar: 'Have + people + -ing' says what the people are doing; 'streaming' means moving in a big steady group.

sentences.context: they started sending in spies to steal his secret recipes
sentences.simple: All the other chocolate makers had begun to feel jealous of the wonderful sweets that Mr Wonka was making, and they began to send spies in to steal his secret recipes.
sentences.grammar: 'Had begun' is the past perfect: it happened before the other past events; 'grow jealous' means 'become jealous'.

sentences.context: chewing-gum that never lost its flavour however much you chewed it
sentences.simple: Then Mr Prodnose's factory began to sell a gum that never lost its taste, no matter how much you chewed it.
sentences.grammar: 'However much you chewed it' means 'no matter how much'; 'came out with' means 'began to sell something new'.

sentences.context: neither Mr Fickelgruber nor Mr Prodnose nor Mr Slugworth nor anybody else is able to copy it
sentences.simple: And now, when Mr Wonka invents a new and wonderful sweet, Mr Fickelgruber, Mr Prodnose, Mr Slugworth and everybody else cannot copy it.
sentences.grammar: 'Neither ... nor ... nor ...' joins the names and makes the whole sentence negative: not one of them can copy it.

sentences.context: whom nobody has seen for the last
sentences.simple: Mr Willy Wonka is a very clever maker of sweets. Nobody has seen him for the last ten years, and today he sent out this notice.
sentences.grammar: 'Whom nobody has seen' tells us about Wonka: nobody has seen him. 'Whom' is the formal word for the person who receives the action.

sentences.context: are the ones who can afford to buy bars of chocolate every day
sentences.simple: The children who find the Golden Tickets will be the ones who have enough money to buy bars of chocolate every day.
sentences.grammar: 'Can afford to + verb' means 'has enough money to'; 'the ones who' means 'the children who'.

sentences.context: go on eating like he does unless he needed nourishment
sentences.simple: And I always say he would not go on eating like this if he did not need food, would he?
sentences.grammar: 'Wouldn't ... unless he needed' means 'only if he needed'; 'would he?' is a tag question that asks you to agree.

sentences.context: I had them loaded on to trucks and sent directly to my own factory
sentences.simple: Then I had people put them on trucks and send them straight to my own factory.
sentences.grammar: 'Had + thing + past participle' ('had them loaded') means someone else did the work for me.

sentences.context: I would keep up the search until I'd got her what she wanted
sentences.simple: I hated to see my little girl so unhappy, so I promised myself that I would go on looking until I got her what she wanted.
sentences.grammar: 'Vowed I would' is a promise made in the past; 'I'd got' means 'I had got'; 'keep up' means 'go on doing'.

sentences.context: however small the chance might be of striking lucky
sentences.simple: The grown-ups also knew one more thing: the chance of getting lucky might be very small, but there was a chance.
sentences.grammar: 'However small the chance might be' means 'no matter how small it is'; 'striking lucky' means 'getting lucky'.

sentences.context: whether he could go on much longer like this without becoming dangerously ill
sentences.simple: It did not seem likely that he could go on like this much longer without getting dangerously ill.
sentences.grammar: 'It seemed doubtful whether' means 'it did not seem sure that'; 'without becoming' means 'and not becoming'.

sentences.context: matter if he spent just one more
sentences.simple: It would not be a problem if he spent just one more…
sentences.grammar: 'If he spent ... it wouldn't matter' is an imagined case (if + past, would + verb), not something real.

sentences.context: I have a feeling you needed a break like this
sentences.simple: I think you needed some good luck like this.
sentences.grammar: 'I have a feeling you needed' leaves out 'that' after 'feeling'; 'a break' here means a lucky chance.

sentences.context: been out of bed these last twenty years
sentences.simple: His long thin body rose up out of the bed, and his bowl of soup flew into the face of Grandma Josephine. In one great jump, this old man of ninety-six and a half, who had not been out of bed for the last twenty years, was on the floor, dancing a winner's dance in his pyjamas.
sentences.grammar: 'Hadn't been ... these last twenty years' is the past perfect: it tells what was true up to the moment when he jumped; 'who' adds extra facts.

sentences.context: Provided, of course, that he feels well enough
sentences.simple: Of course, that is only if he feels well enough.
sentences.grammar: 'Provided that' means 'only if'; the present tense 'feels' is used for something that may happen later.

sentences.context: you will be escorted home by a procession of large trucks
sentences.simple: I, Willy Wonka, will show you around the factory myself and show you everything there is to see. Afterwards, when it is time to leave, a line of large trucks will take you home.
sentences.grammar: 'Will be escorted' is the passive: the trucks will take you, and 'by' names the thing that does it.

sentences.context: no must about it
sentences.simple: It is not a thing that you must do, my dear, Mr Bucket said gently.
sentences.grammar: 'Must' is used as a noun here: 'no must about it' means 'nothing says you must'.

sentences.context: otherwise the whole party might have got out of hand
sentences.simple: All the children, except Charlie, had both their mothers and fathers with them. It was a good thing, or the whole group might have got out of control.
sentences.grammar: 'Otherwise ... might have got' means 'if not, it could have happened'; it did not happen.

sentences.context: a veruca was a sort of wart that you got on the sole of your foot
sentences.simple: I always thought that a veruca was a kind of bump on the skin that you get on the bottom of your foot!
sentences.grammar: 'I always thought that' with 'was' tells what he believed in the past; 'a sort of' means 'a kind of'; 'sole' is the bottom of the foot.

sentences.context: when you came to think of it
sentences.simple: It was quite a large group of people, if you thought about it.
sentences.grammar: 'When you came to think of it' is a fixed phrase that means 'if you think about it'; it gives a new point.

sentences.context: You had only to mention the word
sentences.simple: If you just said the word cacao to an Oompa-Loompa, his mouth would start to run with water.
sentences.grammar: 'You had only to + verb' means 'it was enough to'; 'would' shows what happened every time.

sentences.context: deaf to everything except the call of his enormous stomach
sentences.simple: Augustus could hear nothing except the voice of his big stomach.
sentences.grammar: 'Deaf to' means 'not hearing'; here Augustus pays no attention to anything except 'the call of his stomach', which is his hunger.

sentences.context: liable to get poured out into the fudge boiler
sentences.simple: If you leave him in the chocolate-mixing barrel too long, he may be poured out into the fudge boiler, and that would be a very bad thing, would it not?
sentences.grammar: 'Be liable to + verb' means 'may well happen' (often something bad); 'get poured' is passive: it happens to him.

sentences.context: Whipped cream isn't whipped cream at all unless it's been whipped with whips
sentences.simple: Cream is not whipped cream at all unless someone has whipped it with whips.
sentences.grammar: 'Unless' means 'if not'; 'it's been whipped' is 'it has been whipped', a passive in the present perfect.

sentences.context: He should have burped
sentences.simple: He ought to have burped, Charlie said.
sentences.grammar: 'Should have + past participle' says what was the right thing to do in the past, but it did not happen.

sentences.context: warms you up no end in freezing weather
sentences.simple: Hot ice cream makes you very warm in freezing weather.
sentences.grammar: 'No end' here means 'very much'; 'warms you up' is a phrasal verb that means 'makes you warm'.

sentences.context: there's always a chance that they've decided not to light it today
sentences.simple: There is always a chance that they have decided not to light it today.
sentences.grammar: 'A chance that ...' says what may be true; 'they've decided' is the present perfect: the choice is already made.

sentences.context: as though it had been stung by a wasp
sentences.simple: The doors shut with a loud noise, and the lift jumped away as if a wasp had stung it.
sentences.grammar: 'As though' compares with something imagined; 'had been stung' is the passive past perfect.

sentences.context: children never seem to be able to take it in small doses
sentences.simple: I think it is all right in small amounts, but children never seem able to take it in small amounts.
sentences.grammar: 'Doses' means amounts, like a medicine; 'never seem to be able to' means 'cannot seem to'.

sentences.context: a heck of a long time to come across
sentences.simple: He is taking a very long time to come across, said Mr Teavee, wiping his forehead.
sentences.grammar: 'A heck of a' is informal and means 'a very'; 'come across' here means 'travel from one place to another'.

sentences.context: I had a hunch, you knew, right from the beginning
sentences.simple: I had a feeling from the very start that it would be you!
sentences.grammar: 'A hunch' is a feeling without proof; 'was going to be' looks at the future from a time in the past.

sentences.context: if only for the sake of the Oompa-Loompas
sentences.simple: Someone has to keep it going, even if it is only for the Oompa-Loompas.
sentences.grammar: 'Someone's got to' means 'someone must'; 'if only for' means 'even if it is only for'.

sentences.context: who would give anything for the chance to come in and take over from me
sentences.simple: Mind you, there are thousands of clever men who would give anything for the chance to come in and take over from me, but I do not want that kind of person.
sentences.grammar: 'Would give anything for' means 'want very much'; 'take over from me' means 'start doing my job'.

up one's sleeve.meaning: Kept secret, ready to use later.

look forward to.meaning: To feel happy about something that will come.

save up.meaning: To keep money so that you can buy something later.

go without.meaning: To not have something that you need or want.
go without.example: often went without their own share

go on.meaning: To go on doing something, or to continue.

keep up.meaning: To go on doing something and not stop.

burst into.meaning: To suddenly start to laugh or shout.

make up.meaning: To think of something new, like a song or a story.
make up.example: They are always making up songs.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.

take over.meaning: To start to run something that someone else ran before.

tear off.meaning: To pull something off with force.

come away.meaning: To leave a place and come to the speaker.
come away.example: Come away from that river at once!

hold on.meaning: To keep your hand on something. It can also mean to wait.

hold back.meaning: To stop someone from going forward.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something else.

put on.meaning: To wear something, or to put clothes on your body.

watch out.example: watch out for the Golden Tickets

show off.meaning: To show something to people in a proud way.

shut up.meaning: To stop talking. It is not kind to say this.

come on.meaning: Words that tell someone to go faster or to follow you.

get it over with.example: You might as well get it over with

make way.meaning: To move so that others can pass.

take it easy.meaning: To stay calm and go slowly.

keep calm.meaning: To stay quiet in your mind and not be afraid.

wait and see.meaning: To wait to learn what will happen.

have a hunch.meaning: To have a feeling about something without proof.

in store for.meaning: Waiting to happen to someone in the future.

keep up with.meaning: To go as fast as someone so that you stay with them.

on and on.meaning: For a long time, without stopping.

pick up.meaning: To take something up with your hand.

take off.meaning: To remove clothes or other things.
